title: App Engine Overview
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Understand App Engine as a high-level Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS).

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
App Engine is Google's oldest cloud offering. It allows developers to focus entirely on code without worrying about servers, patches, or networking. It scales automatically from zero to thousands of instances based on traffic. You simply provide your application code and a configuration file (app.yaml).

Environments:
- Standard: For supported languages. Extremely fast scaling, scales to zero (costs $0 when idle).
- Flexible: Runs Docker containers. Best for apps with custom dependencies or non-standard runtimes.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud app versions list` # List versions of App Engine services

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
It provides the fastest 'Time to Market'. If you have a web app in Python, Java, or Go, you can deploy it in one command and let Google handle the rest.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
App Engine is 'Regional'. Once you choose a region for your app, you cannot change it without creating a new project.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Choose the Standard environment for cost-efficiency in supported runtimes, as it can scale down to zero instances during idle periods.

[SUMMARY]
- Fully managed PaaS.
- Zero-server management.
- Automatic scaling and load balancing.
insight: App Engine is 'Regional'. Once you choose a region for your app, you cannot change it without creating a new project.

title: Standard vs. Flexible
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Choose the right App Engine environment for the exam.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
STANDARD ENVIRONMENT:
- Uses sandboxed runtimes (Python, Java, etc.).
- Scales to zero (Cost-effective for low traffic).
- Fast startup (seconds).
- Limited to specific language versions.

FLEXIBLE ENVIRONMENT:
- Uses Docker containers.
- Can use ANY language or library.
- Does NOT scale to zero (minimum 1 instance).
- Slower startup (minutes) because it boots GCE VMs under the hood.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'runtime: python39' > app.yaml` # Create a basic app.yaml config

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Standard is ideal for startups and low-budget projects needing auto-scaling. Flexible is necessary for enterprise apps with custom OS requirements or non-standard languages.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Assuming Flexible scales to zero. It always maintains at least one instance, which can lead to unexpected costs for idle apps.

[BEST PRACTICE]
If the requirement is 'Cost-effective' and 'Scales to zero', choose Standard. If the requirement is 'Custom binary' or 'Docker', choose Flexible.

[SUMMARY]
Standard for cost and speed; Flexible for customization and full Docker support.
insight: Flexible environment is essentially a managed group of VMs—you can even SSH into them for debugging.

title: Deploying with gcloud app
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Master the deployment workflow for App Engine.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
To deploy, you need an app.yaml file in your source directory. GCP packages your code, uploads it to a bucket, builds the container, and starts the service. Every deployment creates a new Version, allowing for safe testing and traffic management.

Traffic Splitting: By default, the new version gets 100% of traffic. You can use the --no-promote flag to deploy a version without sending it traffic immediately.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud app deploy` # Deploy the application
* `gcloud app services list` # List all services in the app
* `gcloud app versions stop [ID]` # Stop a specific version
* `gcloud app deploy --no-promote` # Deploy without promoting to 100% traffic

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Deploying a new feature version in 'isolation' using --no-promote, testing it with a specific URL, then shifting traffic when ready.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Forgetting that the first 'app deploy' sets the project region permanently. Choosing the wrong region can affect latency for your users.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Always use versions for rollbacks. If a new deployment fails, you can immediately switch traffic back to the previous stable version.

[SUMMARY]
- `gcloud app deploy` is the primary command.
- Versions allow for safe rollbacks.
- app.yaml is the mandatory config file.
insight: The first time you run 'app deploy' in a project, Google will ask you to choose a region. Choose carefully!

title: Cloud Run (Serverless Containers)
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Deploy stateless containers on a fully managed platform.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Cloud Run is the modern middle ground, combining the ease of App Engine with the flexibility of Docker. You provide a container image (stored in Artifact Registry), and Cloud Run runs it as a web service. It is a managed Knative service that scales to zero and charges only when your container processes requests.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud run services list` # List all Cloud Run services

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Ideal for modern microservices and APIs. It's portable (standard Docker) but has zero operational overhead, making it perfect for rapid development and deployment.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Trying to use Cloud Run for stateful apps. Cloud Run is 'Stateless'; local disk writes are lost when the instance scales down or restarts.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Ensure your application can start quickly to minimize latency during 'cold starts' when scaling from zero.

[SUMMARY]
- Managed Knative (Kubernetes-based).
- Scales to zero.
- Uses standard Docker images.
insight: Cloud Run is 'Stateless'. You cannot save files to the local disk and expect them to be there for the next request.

title: Deploying to Cloud Run
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Perform your first container deployment to Cloud Run.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
The workflow involves building your Docker image, pushing it to Artifact Registry, and then running the deploy command. By default, services are private. Cloud Run can also run 'Jobs'—containers that run to completion and exit.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud run deploy [NAME] --image=[IMAGE_URL] --region=us-central1` # Deploy from image
* `gcloud run deploy [NAME] --image=[IMAGE_URL] --allow-unauthenticated` # Deploy public service
* `gcloud run deploy --source .` # Build and deploy from source code

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Deploying a public web-frontend or an internal batch processing job that runs on a schedule.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Deploying without specifying a region, which might result in the service being placed in a suboptimal location relative to your data or users.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use `--allow-unauthenticated` only for public-facing services. Keep internal APIs private and use IAM for secure access.

[SUMMARY]
- `gcloud run deploy` is the primary command.
- Requires images in Artifact Registry.
- Region must be specified.
insight: Cloud Run can also run 'Jobs'—containers that run to completion and exit, perfect for database migrations.

title: Cloud Run Traffic Splitting
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Implement Canary deployments and rollbacks in Cloud Run.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Every deployment to Cloud Run creates a new immutable Revision. You can split traffic between these revisions, allowing for safe rollouts. Revisions not receiving traffic are not charged for storage or CPU.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud run services update-traffic [NAME] --to-revisions=[REV1]=50,[REV2]=50` # 50/50 split
* `gcloud run revisions list --service=[NAME]` # List all revisions

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Canary releases: Send 90% of users to the stable 'Revision-A' and 10% to the new 'Revision-B'. If the new feature fails, rollback 100% to 'Revision-A' instantly.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Assuming you need to re-deploy to rollback. You just need to shift traffic back to an existing, immutable revision.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Always verify the health of a new revision with a small percentage of traffic before shifting the full load.

[SUMMARY]
- Revisions are immutable snapshots.
- Traffic can be split by percentage.
- Enables zero-downtime 'Canary' releases.
insight: Revisions that are not receiving traffic are NOT charged for storage or CPU.

title: GKE Overview (Kubernetes)
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Understand Google Kubernetes Engine as a managed K8s service.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
GKE is the most powerful compute option, managing clusters of VMs (Nodes) to automate deployment, scaling, and health of containers. 

Components:
- Control Plane: Managed by Google (The Brain).
- Nodes: VMs that run your containers (The Muscle).

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud container clusters list` # List all GKE clusters

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Ideal for complex microservices architectures, stateful applications (databases), or workloads requiring specific hardware like GPUs.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Choosing GKE for simple web apps that could run on Cloud Run. GKE has a higher management overhead and cost floor.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use GKE for complex orchestration needs, but start with Cloud Run for simpler, stateless containerized services.

[SUMMARY]
- Managed Kubernetes service.
- Highest level of control and complexity.
- Best for microservices and stateful apps.
insight: GKE is the 'Heavy Lifter'—if you have complex networking or need GPUs for containers, use GKE.
next: GKE Cluster Modes: Autopilot vs Standard

title: GKE Autopilot vs. Standard
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Choose the right GKE mode for operational efficiency.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
AUTOPILOT (Recommended):
- Google manages nodes, OS, and security.
- Pay only for the Pods you run (CPU/RAM per pod).
- Enforces security best practices by default.

STANDARD:
- You manage node pools (VM types, disk size).
- Pay for the VMs (Nodes) regardless of Pod count.
- Best for fine-grained control or high-utilization clusters.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud container clusters create-auto [NAME] --region=[REGION]` # Create Autopilot cluster

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Use Autopilot to reduce operational burden for standard apps. Use Standard if you need to optimize node utilization for cost or need custom kernel modules.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Over-provisioning nodes in Standard mode, leading to wasted costs. Autopilot eliminates this risk by billing per pod.

[BEST PRACTICE]
If the question asks for 'Reduced operational overhead' or 'Pay-per-pod', the answer is Autopilot.

[SUMMARY]
Autopilot for simplicity and pod-based billing; Standard for full control over nodes.
insight: Autopilot enforces security best practices by default (e.g., no privileged containers).

title: Creating a GKE Cluster
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Provision a Kubernetes cluster via CLI.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
You must choose between Zonal and Regional availability:
- Zonal: One control plane in one zone. Outages in that zone freeze cluster management.
- Regional: Three control planes in three zones. Highest availability (SLA 99.95%).

Clusters should be 'VPC-Native' (uses Alias IPs) for better integration with GCP services.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud container clusters create [NAME] --region=us-central1 --num-nodes=3` # Create regional cluster
* `gcloud container clusters list` # List clusters and their status

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Production workloads should always use Regional clusters to ensure management availability during single-zone failures.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Not realizing that a regional cluster with `--num-nodes=3` creates 3 nodes PER zone (9 nodes total), which can significantly impact your bill.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Always ensure the cluster is 'VPC-Native' for improved security and performance with internal GCP load balancers.

[SUMMARY]
- Regional clusters are best for production.
- VPC-Native networking is the standard.
- Control Plane is managed by Google.
insight: A regional cluster actually creates 3 nodes per zone (9 nodes total) by default if you specify --num-nodes=3.

title: Configuring kubectl
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Connect your local terminal to the GKE cluster.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
While gcloud manages the infrastructure (VMs/Clusters), kubectl manages the workloads inside the cluster (Pods/Deployments). You must 'get credentials' to update your local kubeconfig with the API endpoint and security certificates. GKE uses your GCP identity for authentication.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud container clusters get-credentials [NAME] --region=[REGION]` # Get cluster auth
* `kubectl get nodes` # Verify connection to nodes

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
An engineer using Cloud Shell to quickly inspect a running production cluster without having to manually manage certificates.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Trying to use kubectl without running get-credentials first, resulting in 'Connection Refused' or 'The connection to the server localhost:8080 was refused'.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Always verify your connection with `kubectl get nodes` after switching contexts or getting credentials.

[SUMMARY]
- `gcloud` = Manage the cluster (Infrastructure).
- `kubectl` = Manage the workloads (Pods/Deployments).
- `get-credentials` is the bridge between the two.
insight: In Cloud Shell, kubectl is already installed and often pre-configured for your active project.

title: Kubernetes Pods
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Understand the atomic unit of Kubernetes.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
A Pod is the smallest unit of work in K8s, wrapping one or more containers that share the same network IP and storage. Pods are ephemeral; if they crash or the node fails, K8s deletes them and creates a brand new one elsewhere.

[COMMANDS]
* `kubectl get pods` # List all pods in namespace
* `kubectl describe pod [NAME]` # View deep details and events
* `kubectl logs [NAME]` # See stdout/stderr from container

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Debugging an application by checking its logs or describing the pod to see if it failed because of 'Insufficient memory'.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Creating a Pod directly for production. Pods are not self-healing on their own; if they die, they stay dead unless managed by a Deployment.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Never create a Pod directly; always use a 'Deployment' to manage pod lifecycles and scaling.

[SUMMARY]
- Wrapper for containers.
- Shared network/storage.
- Ephemeral and replaceable.
insight: Never create a Pod directly for production; always use a 'Deployment' to manage them.

title: Kubernetes Deployments
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Manage scaling and updates for your containers.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
A Deployment is a controller that maintains a desired state of Pods. It handles replica counts, self-healing (restarting pods on healthy nodes), and zero-downtime rolling updates when the container image changes.

[COMMANDS]
* `kubectl create deployment [NAME] --image=[IMAGE]` # Create deployment
* `kubectl scale deployment [NAME] --replicas=10` # Scale replicas
* `kubectl get deployments` # View deployment status

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Rolling out a new version of a web-server. The Deployment creates new pods with the new image one-by-one, ensuring users never see an outage.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Manual scaling of pods. Always scale the Deployment, not the individual pods, so the desired state is maintained by Kubernetes.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use `kubectl apply -f [YAML]` for deployments instead of `kubectl create` to enable declarative infrastructure management.

[SUMMARY]
- Manages replica counts.
- Handles self-healing (restarts Pods).
- Automates rolling updates.
insight: A Deployment uses a 'ReplicaSet' under the hood to handle the actual count of Pods.

title: Kubernetes Services
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Provide stable endpoints for ephemeral Pods.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Since Pod IPs change, Services provide a stable IP and DNS name for a group of Pods, acting as an internal load balancer. They use 'Labels and Selectors' to identify their target pods.

Types:
1. ClusterIP: Internal only (default).
2. NodePort: Opens port on every node IP.
3. LoadBalancer: Creates a GCP Network Load Balancer with a public IP.

[COMMANDS]
* `kubectl get services` # List services and external IPs
* `kubectl expose deployment [NAME] --type=LoadBalancer --port=80` # Expose app

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Using a ClusterIP service for a backend database so only the frontend pods can reach it, and a LoadBalancer service for the frontend to be reachable by users.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Thinking ClusterIP services are reachable from the internet. They are internal to the cluster only.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use 'LoadBalancer' type for production apps needing public access, as it integrates automatically with GCP infrastructure.

[SUMMARY]
- Stable IP/DNS for Pods.
- Load balances traffic internally.
- 'LoadBalancer' type creates a real cloud resource.
insight: Services use 'Labels and Selectors' to know which Pods belong to them.

title: GKE Node Pools
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Manage sets of VMs with different hardware specs.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
A cluster can have multiple Node Pools, which are sets of identical VMs. This allows you to run different workloads on specialized hardware (e.g., standard VMs for web, GPU VMs for AI) within the same cluster.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud container node-pools list --cluster=[NAME]` # List pools
* `gcloud container node-pools create gpu-pool --cluster=[NAME] --machine-type=n1-standard-4 --accelerator=type=nvidia-tesla-t4,count=1` # Add specialized pool

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Running a 'standard-pool' of cheap E2 VMs for the application frontend and a 'gpu-pool' for intensive machine learning tasks.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Leaving the 'default-pool' at its original size if you have created specialized pools. The default-pool can often be deleted or downsized to save costs.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use node pools to segment workloads that require different CPU/Memory ratios or specific hardware like SSDs or GPUs.

[SUMMARY]
- Subset of nodes in a cluster.
- Allows for hardware specialization.
- Can be auto-scaled individually.
insight: The 'default-pool' is created automatically with the cluster. Many engineers delete it and create custom pools immediately.

title: GKE Cluster Autoscaler
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Automatically scale the number of VMs in your cluster.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
The Cluster Autoscaler monitors for 'Pending' Pods that cannot be scheduled due to lack of resources. It then triggers Compute Engine to add more VMs to the pool. It also removes underutilized nodes to save money.

Difference:
- HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler): Adds Pods (Software level).
- Cluster Autoscaler: Adds VMs (Hardware level).

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud container clusters update [NAME] --enable-autoscaling --min-nodes=1 --max-nodes=10` # Enable autoscaling

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A sudden spike in traffic causes Pods to scale out. Once the existing nodes are full, the Cluster Autoscaler adds new nodes so the pending Pods can start.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Assuming HPA is enough. If you have many Pods but no physical VM space, those Pods will stay in 'Pending' state forever unless the Cluster Autoscaler is active.

[BEST PRACTICE]
On the exam: If Pods are 'Pending' due to 'Insufficient CPU', the answer is to enable or increase the Cluster Autoscaler.

[SUMMARY]
- Scales the number of Nodes (VMs).
- Triggered by resource demand (CPU/RAM requests).
- Critical for cost-effective GKE production clusters.
insight: On the exam: If Pods are 'Pending' due to 'Insufficient CPU', the answer is to enable or increase the Cluster Autoscaler.

title: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA)
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Automatically scale the number of application replicas.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
HPA monitors resource usage (like CPU) and adjusts the number of Pod replicas in a Deployment. It requires 'Resource Requests' to be defined in the Pod manifest so it knows the baseline for usage.

[COMMANDS]
* `kubectl autoscale deployment [NAME] --cpu-percent=80 --min=2 --max=10` # Create HPA
* `kubectl get hpa` # View HPA status

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A web application that scales from 2 pods during the night to 10 pods during the midday traffic peak, maintaining an 80% CPU target.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Setting up HPA without defining resource requests in your container spec. HPA will not be able to calculate percentages and will fail to scale.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Always define CPU and Memory 'requests' and 'limits' for your containers to ensure predictable HPA behavior.

[SUMMARY]
- Scales the number of Pods.
- Based on real-time metrics (CPU/RAM).
- Prevents application slowness during traffic spikes.
insight: HPA can also scale based on custom metrics like 'requests per second' from a Load Balancer.

title: GKE Workload Identity
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Securely connect containers to GCP APIs.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Workload Identity is the gold standard for GKE security. It links a Kubernetes Service Account (KSA) to a Google Cloud Service Account (GSA). The container 'becomes' the GSA and gets temporary tokens, eliminating the need for insecure static JSON keys on disk.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'IAM Binding: K8S_SA -> GCP_SA'` # Concept of identity linking

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A pod running in GKE needs to upload images to a Cloud Storage bucket. Instead of storing a secret key, the pod uses its GSA identity to authenticate seamlessly.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Downloading service account JSON keys and storing them in Kubernetes Secrets. This is less secure and creates a management burden for key rotation.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Always use Workload Identity for any application running in GKE that needs to access other GCP services like Storage, Pub/Sub, or Spanner.

[SUMMARY]
- Preferred way to handle GKE-to-GCP auth.
- No static JSON keys.
- Granular permissions per-application.
insight: Workload Identity is required in Autopilot and strongly recommended in Standard.

title: GKE Private Clusters
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Isolate your cluster from the public internet.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
In a Private Cluster, nodes do not have public IP addresses and are invisible to the internet. You must configure 'Authorized Networks' to allow management access to the Control Plane and use Cloud NAT for outbound internet access from containers.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud container clusters describe [NAME] --format='get(privateClusterConfig)'` # Check private config

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Enterprise workloads that must comply with strict security standards, ensuring that internal services are never exposed to external probes.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Deploying a private cluster and forgetting to set up Cloud NAT. Your containers will be unable to download security patches or external libraries.

[BEST PRACTICE]
On the exam: To increase the security posture of a GKE cluster, the best answer is to make it a Private Cluster.

[SUMMARY]
- Nodes have internal IPs only.
- High security for enterprise workloads.
- Requires 'Authorized Networks' for management access.
insight: On the exam: To increase the security posture of a GKE cluster, the best answer is to make it a Private Cluster.

title: Artifact Registry
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Store and manage container images and packages.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Artifact Registry is the successor to Container Registry (GCR). It supports Docker images, Maven/npm packages, and Python modules. It offers regional storage, vulnerability scanning, and IAM integration for fine-grained access control.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud artifacts repositories create [NAME] --repository-format=docker --location=[LOC]` # Create repo
* `gcloud auth configure-docker [LOC]-docker.pkg.dev` # Auth docker
* `gcloud artifacts repositories list` # List all repos

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Storing your company's private Docker images close to your GKE clusters in `us-central1` for faster deployment and reduced data egress costs.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Continuing to use the older Container Registry (GCR) for new projects. Artifact Registry is more feature-rich and is the recommended platform.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Enable automated vulnerability scanning to catch security holes in your images as soon as they are pushed.

[SUMMARY]
- Managed private registry.
- Supports many package types (Docker, npm, etc.).
- Integrated vulnerability scanning.
insight: Always use Artifact Registry instead of Container Registry for new projects—it is more flexible and feature-rich.

title: Cloud Build (Automation)
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Automate the build, test, and deploy process.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Cloud Build is a serverless CI/CD platform that executes your build in defined steps. Each step is a Docker container. You define the pipeline in a cloudbuild.yaml file. It integrates with GitHub for automated triggers upon code push.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud builds submit --config cloudbuild.yaml .` # Submit manual build
* `gcloud builds list --limit=1` # View latest build status

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Automatically building a new Docker image, pushing it to Artifact Registry, and deploying it to GKE every time a developer merges code into the 'main' branch.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Not using caches in your build steps. Cloud Build can be significantly faster if you leverage build caches for layers and dependencies.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Keep your build steps modular and use standard Google-provided builder images for common tasks like `gcloud` or `docker`.

[SUMMARY]
- Serverless CI/CD.
- Step-based execution.
- Integrated with Artifact Registry and Cloud Run.
insight: Cloud Build is extremely fast because it runs on Google's private network with access to high-speed caches.

title: ConfigMaps & Secrets
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Decouple configuration from container images.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
ConfigMaps are for non-sensitive data (e.g., config files, environment names). Secrets are for sensitive data (e.g., API keys, passwords). Both allow the same container image to run in different environments (Dev, Prod) without modification.

[COMMANDS]
* `kubectl create configmap my-config --from-literal=env=prod` # Create config
* `kubectl create secret generic db-pass --from-literal=password=123` # Create secret

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
In Dev, a pod uses a ConfigMap that points to a test database. In Prod, the same pod uses a ConfigMap pointing to the production database and a Secret for the password.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Thinking Kubernetes Secrets are fully encrypted by default. They are only Base64 encoded! Anyone with access to the cluster can easily decode them.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Enable 'Application-layer Secrets Encryption' in GKE to protect your secrets with a Cloud KMS key for real production security.

[SUMMARY]
- ConfigMaps = Public config.
- Secrets = Private/Sensitive config.
- Allows the same image to run in Dev, Staging, and Prod.
insight: Kubernetes Secrets are only Base64 encoded, not encrypted by default! Enable 'Application-layer Secrets Encryption' in GKE for real security.

title: Kubernetes Namespaces
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Partition a single cluster for multi-tenancy.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
A Namespace is a virtual cluster inside a physical cluster. It isolates resources between teams or environments (Dev/Prod), allowing for resource quotas and avoiding naming collisions between different services.

[COMMANDS]
* `kubectl get ns` # List all namespaces
* `kubectl create namespace [NAME]` # Create new namespace
* `kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=[NAME]` # Switch namespace

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Using one cluster but giving each development team their own namespace so they can't accidentally delete each other's pods.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Running everything in the 'default' namespace. This leads to clutter and makes it impossible to apply granular resource limits per team.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Always use dedicated namespaces for production workloads and apply ResourceQuotas to prevent one app from exhausting cluster resources.

[SUMMARY]
- Logical isolation within a cluster.
- Supports resource limits and quotas.
- Good for multi-team environments.
insight: The 'default' namespace is where everything goes if you don't specify one. Don't use it for production!

lab.output:
NAME          STATUS
default       Active
kube-system   Active

title: GKE Ingress
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Expose multiple GKE services via one Load Balancer.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
While a LoadBalancer service creates one IP per app (Layer 4), Ingress is a Layer 7 controller that uses rules (Path/Host) to route traffic to multiple internal services through a single Global HTTP(S) Load Balancer.

[COMMANDS]
* `kubectl get ingress` # View ingress status and IP

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
One Load Balancer serving `mysite.com/api` (Service A) and `mysite.com/blog` (Service B). This saves money and allows for centralized SSL management.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Trying to use Ingress without the 'HTTP Load Balancing' add-on enabled on the GKE cluster. The Ingress object will be created but will never get an IP.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use Ingress for web applications to benefit from Google-managed SSL certificates and Cloud Armor security protection.

[SUMMARY]
- Layer 7 external access.
- Path-based and Host-based routing.
- Uses the Google Global HTTP(S) Load Balancer.
insight: To use Ingress in GKE, you must have the 'HTTP Load Balancing' add-on enabled on your cluster.

title: Cloud Functions
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Execute code in response to cloud events.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Cloud Functions is Function-as-a-Service (FaaS). You provide code (JS, Python, Go) that triggers based on events like HTTP requests, GCS file uploads, Pub/Sub messages, or Firestore changes.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud functions list` # List all deployed functions

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Automated thumbnail generation: When a user uploads a high-res photo to a GCS bucket, a Cloud Function is triggered to create and store a smaller version automatically.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Using Cloud Functions for long-running tasks. They have a maximum timeout of 9 minutes. For longer tasks, use Cloud Run or GKE.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Keep functions stateless and focused on a single task to take full advantage of their rapid scaling and cost-efficiency.

[SUMMARY]
- Pure serverless code.
- Event-driven execution.
- Zero scaling management.
insight: Cloud Functions are best for short-running tasks (max 9 minutes). If your task takes longer, use Cloud Run.

title: Deploying Cloud Functions
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Master the deployment flags for serverless functions.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
When deploying, you must specify the runtime and the trigger type. Second-gen functions run on Cloud Run, providing better performance and more concurrency options.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud functions deploy [NAME] --runtime=[RUNTIME] --trigger-http --allow-unauthenticated` # Public HTTP function
* `gcloud functions deploy [NAME] --runtime=python311 --trigger-resource=[BUCKET] --trigger-event=google.storage.object.finalize` # GCS trigger

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Deploying a simple webhook that receives data from an external service and stores it in BigQuery.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Deploying without the `--allow-unauthenticated` flag for a public API, resulting in '403 Forbidden' errors for external users.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use 2nd Gen Cloud Functions for new projects as they offer longer timeouts, larger instance sizes, and better performance.

[SUMMARY]
- Specify runtime and trigger.
- Supports environment variables.
- `allow-unauthenticated` makes HTTP functions public.
insight: Cloud Functions (2nd gen) actually runs on top of Cloud Run under the hood, giving it better performance.

title: Liveness vs. Readiness Probes
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Differentiate between application health signals in GKE.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
READINESS PROBE: Checks if the app is ready to handle traffic. If it fails, K8s stops sending traffic to that pod. Use this while the app is loading data.
LIVENESS PROBE: Checks if the app is alive. If it fails, K8s kills the pod and starts a fresh one. Use this to catch deadlocks.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'livenessProbe: {httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8080}}'` # YAML config snippet

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
An application that needs 30 seconds to load a large cache should use a Readiness probe so it doesn't receive user requests until it is fully ready.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Using a Liveness probe to check for backend database health. If the DB goes down, all your pods will crash-loop, which doesn't fix the DB and makes the outage worse!

[BEST PRACTICE]
Always implement at least a Readiness probe to ensure your users never get '502 Bad Gateway' errors during app startup or scaling.

[SUMMARY]
- Readiness = Handle traffic?
- Liveness = Alive or stuck?
- Probes defined in container spec.
insight: Don't use a Liveness probe to check for backend database health, or your app will reboot in an infinite loop if the DB is down!

title: GKE Resource Quotas
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Prevent 'Noisy Neighbors' from crashing your cluster.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Resource Quotas are applied to a Namespace to limit the total CPU/RAM all pods can use. Resource Limits are applied to individual pods:
- Requests: Guaranteed resources.
- Limits: Absolute maximum before being throttled or killed.

[COMMANDS]
* `kubectl get resourcequotas` # List quotas in namespace

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Limiting the 'development' namespace to 4 CPUs so that a developer's infinite loop doesn't steal resources from the 'production' namespace.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Not setting limits on containers. A single pod with a memory leak can 'starve' the entire node, crashing other innocent pods.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Set realistic 'Requests' based on average usage and 'Limits' to prevent catastrophic resource exhaustion.

[SUMMARY]
- Quotas protect the Namespace.
- Limits protect the Node.
- Prevents one application from starving others.
insight: In GKE Autopilot, Google automatically sets these for you based on your Pod sizes.

title: GKE Maintenance Windows
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Control when Google upgrades your cluster.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Google periodically updates the Control Plane and Nodes. Maintenance Windows let you define specific times (e.g., Sundays at 2 AM) for these tasks. Maintenance Exclusions allow you to 'freeze' upgrades for up to 30 days during critical business periods.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud container clusters update [NAME] --maintenance-window=[TIME] --maintenance-window-duration=4h` # Set window
* `gcloud container clusters describe [NAME] --format='get(maintenancePolicy)'` # View policy

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Setting a 30-day maintenance exclusion during 'Black Friday' and 'Cyber Monday' to ensure no infrastructure changes occur during peak shopping season.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Not setting a window and having a cluster upgrade occur during your busiest hour, potentially causing transient service disruptions.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Align your maintenance windows with your team's on-call schedule so someone is available if an automated upgrade causes issues.

[SUMMARY]
- Controls timing of automated upgrades.
- Essential for preventing mid-day downtime.
- Can exclude specific dates entirely.
insight: Even with maintenance windows, Google may bypass them for 'Critical' security emergencies.

title: Binary Authorization
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Enforce container security at deployment time.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Binary Authorization ensures only 'signed' and verified images can run in GKE. You define a policy requiring an 'Attestation' (signature) from a trusted system (like Cloud Build) before deployment is allowed.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'Policy: Disallow All, Except Signed Images'` # Concept of enforcement

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
An enterprise requirement that only images which have passed a security scan in the CI/CD pipeline are allowed to be deployed to the production cluster.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Deploying without attestations after enabling Binary Authorization. All your deployments will fail until the images are properly signed.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use Binary Authorization as part of a 'Secure Supply Chain' to prevent unauthorized or malicious code from entering your environment.

[SUMMARY]
- Deploy-time security check.
- Requires 'Attestations' (Signatures).
- Prevents unauthorized image execution.
insight: Binary Authorization is a key requirement for companies seeking 'Supply Chain Security' (SLSA) compliance.

title: GKE Cost Optimization
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Reduce GKE spend without sacrificing performance.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Techniques include:
1. Autopilot: Zero waste billing.
2. Spot Nodes: Up to 90% discount for fault-tolerant tasks.
3. Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA): Right-sizes pod resource requests automatically.
4. Namespace Quotas: Limits per-team spending.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud container node-pools create spot-pool --cluster=[NAME] --spot` # Create spot pool

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Running a large-scale batch data processing job on Spot VMs to save thousands of dollars, knowing the job can handle occasional node preemption.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Over-estimating pod resource requests. This 'blocks' space on nodes that other pods could use, leading to an unnecessarily large and expensive cluster.

[BEST PRACTICE]
A common ACE exam question asks how to run a 'Batch' job on GKE for the lowest price—the answer is 'Spot VMs'.

[SUMMARY]
- Spot nodes for cost savings.
- VPA for right-sizing.
- Autopilot for simplicity and efficiency.
insight: A common ACE exam question asks how to run a 'Batch' job on GKE for the lowest price—the answer is 'Spot VMs'.

title: Cloud Deploy
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Automate the promotion of code through environments.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Cloud Deploy is a managed Continuous Delivery service for GKE and Cloud Run. It defines a Delivery Pipeline (e.g., Dev -> Staging -> Prod) with built-in logic for one-click promotion, rollbacks, and mandatory approvals for production targets.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud deploy delivery-pipelines list` # List pipelines

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A release manager reviewing and 'Approving' a deployment to the Production cluster after the Staging tests have passed successfully.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Confusing Cloud Build with Cloud Deploy. Build is for creating the artifact; Deploy is for managing the movement of that artifact through environments.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Always require manual approval for the Production target to add a layer of human verification before live changes.

[SUMMARY]
- Managed CD service.
- Environment promotion logic.
- Built-in rollbacks and approvals.
insight: Cloud Deploy keeps an audit log of every person who promoted code to Production—great for compliance.

title: Regional Clusters (HA)
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Design clusters for 99.99% availability.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Zonal Cluster: Control plane in one zone. If that zone fails, you cannot scale or manage the cluster.
Regional Cluster: Control plane replicated across 3 zones. The cluster remains fully operational even during a total zone failure. Nodes are also spread across zones automatically.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud container clusters describe [NAME] --format='get(location)'` # Check if regional

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Mission-critical applications that must remain manageable and scalable even during major infrastructure outages in a specific data center zone.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Choosing Zonal for production to save the management fee. The risk of losing cluster management during an outage far outweighs the small cost savings.

[BEST PRACTICE]
On the ACE exam: If the goal is 'High Availability', the answer is almost always a Regional resource.

[SUMMARY]
- Regional = 3 Control Planes.
- Zonal = 1 Control Plane.
- Use Regional for anything that shouldn't go down.
insight: On the ACE exam: If the goal is 'High Availability', the answer is almost always a Regional resource.

title: Multi-cluster Ingress
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Scale Kubernetes across multiple GCP regions.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Multi-cluster Ingress (MCI) allows a global load balancer to treat multiple GKE clusters as a single backend. It uses a 'Config Cluster' to store rules and directs users to the nearest healthy pod in ANY cluster across the globe.

[COMMANDS]
* `echo 'Configured via MultiClusterIngress YAML'` # Configuration method

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A truly global app with one cluster in US and one in Europe. MCI ensures US users hit the US cluster and European users hit the European one, providing low latency and regional failover.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Thinking standard Ingress can cross regions. Standard Ingress is local to one cluster; MCI is required for multi-cluster/multi-region load balancing.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use MCI for disaster recovery strategies where an entire GCP region failure is part of your threat model.

[SUMMARY]
- Global load balancing across clusters.
- Disaster recovery at the regional level.
- Low latency for global users.
insight: MCI is an advanced feature often used by enterprises with strict uptime requirements.

title: Container Analysis
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Automate the security auditing of your Docker images.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
The Container Analysis API automatically scans images in Artifact Registry for known vulnerabilities (CVEs), assigning severity scores (Critical to Low). You can trigger build failures if 'Critical' vulnerabilities are found.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud artifacts docker images list-vulnerabilities [IMAGE_PATH]` # List scan results

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Integrating security into the dev workflow by blocking any deployment that uses an image with a 'High' or 'Critical' vulnerability.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Thinking scanning stops the deployment. It is a 'Passive' check; you must use it in combination with Binary Authorization to actually block deployments.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Regularly review scanning reports to ensure your base images are kept up to date with the latest security patches.

[SUMMARY]
- Automated security scanning.
- Integrates with Artifact Registry.
- Foundation for Binary Authorization.
insight: Container scanning is a 'Passive' check—it doesn't stop the deploy unless you use it with Binary Authorization.

title: App Engine Cron Jobs
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Schedule periodic tasks in a serverless environment.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
App Engine has a built-in scheduler defined in cron.yaml using standard cron syntax. At the scheduled time, App Engine sends an internal HTTP GET request to a specific URL in your app to trigger the task logic.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud app deploy cron.yaml` # Deploy cron config
* `echo 'cron:
- description: daily cleanup
  url: /tasks/cleanup
  schedule: every 24 hours' > cron.yaml` # Example config

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Performing a daily database cleanup or syncing user data with an external CRM API every midnight.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Expecting cron jobs to work without an active App Engine service. The job depends on your app being able to receive the HTTP trigger.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Secure your cron handler URLs so only the App Engine Cron service (IP 0.1.0.2) can trigger them.

[SUMMARY]
- Automated task scheduling.
- Defined in cron.yaml.
- Triggers via internal HTTP requests.
insight: GCP also has a standalone service called 'Cloud Scheduler' which can trigger Cloud Run or Cloud Functions without needing App Engine.

title: GKE Workload Identity Setup
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Understand the technical steps of identity linking in GKE.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
The 'Handshake' involves:
1. Enabling Workload Identity on the cluster.
2. Creating a Google Service Account (GSA) with GCP roles.
3. Creating a Kubernetes Service Account (KSA) in the namespace.
4. Binding the KSA to the GSA via IAM policy.
5. Annotating the KSA to link it to the GSA.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding [GSA] --role roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser --member "serviceAccount:[PROJECT].svc.id.goog[[NS]/[KSA]]"` # Bind identities

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Ensuring that only the 'payment-service' in the 'prod' namespace has permission to write to the 'payments' Cloud Spanner database.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Missing the annotation step. Even if the IAM binding is correct, Kubernetes won't know which identity to assume without the `iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account` annotation.

[BEST PRACTICE]
On the exam: Workload Identity is the answer for ANY question about 'Securely accessing GCP services from GKE'.

[SUMMARY]
- GSA = GCP Permissions.
- KSA = Kubernetes Identity.
- Binding links them securely.
insight: On the exam: Workload Identity is the answer for ANY question about 'Securely accessing GCP services from GKE'.

title: Pod Troubleshooting
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Use describe and logs to find deployment errors in Kubernetes.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Common Failures:
- ImagePullBackOff: Bad image name or no registry permissions.
- CrashLoopBackOff: App starts but crashes immediately (bugs/missing config).
- Pending: No node has enough CPU/RAM.

[COMMANDS]
* `kubectl get pods` # Check status
* `kubectl describe pod [NAME]` # Check 'Events' for error messages
* `kubectl logs [NAME]` # Check app internal output
* `kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp` # Timeline of errors

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Diagnosing why a new deployment is stuck in 'Pending' by using `describe` and finding that the pod requested 4 CPUs when the nodes only have 2.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Checking only `kubectl get pods`. It tells you the status but not the 'Why'. Always check `describe` and `logs` for the root cause.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Use `kubectl describe` for Kubernetes infrastructure errors and `kubectl logs` for application-level code errors.

[SUMMARY]
- `describe` for K8s errors.
- `logs` for application errors.
- Check Events for scheduling failures.
insight: Use 'kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp' to see a timeline of what went wrong in your cluster.

title: Auto-repair & Auto-upgrade
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Enable GKE's 'Self-Healing' nodes for operational stability.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Auto-repair: Google monitors node health (Kubelet/Disk) and recreates unhealthy VMs automatically.
Auto-upgrade: Keeps nodes on the latest stable K8s version for security and feature parity. These are ON by default in Autopilot and highly recommended for Standard.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud container node-pools update [POOL] --cluster=[NAME] --enable-autorepair --enable-autoupgrade` # Enable self-healing
* `gcloud container node-pools describe [POOL] --cluster=[NAME] --format='get(management)'` # Verify status

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
A node experiences a sudden hardware failure at 3 AM. GKE Auto-repair detects it, deletes the VM, and spins up a new one without any human intervention.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Disabling auto-upgrade to 'prevent breaking changes' but then forgetting to manually patch nodes, leaving the cluster vulnerable to security exploits.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Always keep Auto-repair enabled to minimize downtime from unpredictable hardware or OS-level failures.

[SUMMARY]
- Nodes fix themselves (Auto-repair).
- Nodes stay current (Auto-upgrade).
- Essential for reducing maintenance 'Drift'.
insight: Auto-repair and Auto-upgrade are ON by default in GKE Autopilot.

title: Cloud Run Domains
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Connect your own domain to a serverless service.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Cloud Run allows you to map custom domains (e.g., myapp.com) to replace default URLs. Google automatically provisions free Managed SSL certificates for these domains. If mapping isn't available in a region, use a Global HTTP(S) Load Balancer.

[COMMANDS]
* `gcloud beta run domain-mappings create --service [NAME] --domain [DOMAIN]` # Map domain
* `gcloud beta run domain-mappings list` # View mappings

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Setting up a production URL for a new startup's web app on Cloud Run, ensuring it has 'HTTPS' active and a professional `.com` domain.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Trying to map a domain in a region that doesn't support it yet. Always check the GCP documentation for the latest regional availability of domain mapping.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Cloud Run is the only serverless service with built-in, easy domain mapping and SSL (App Engine also has it, but it is much older).

[SUMMARY]
- Replaces default .run.app URL.
- Includes free managed SSL.
- Limited regional availability.
insight: Cloud Run is the only serverless service with built-in, easy domain mapping and SSL (App Engine also has it, but it is much older).

title: Deployment Summary
content:
[OBJECTIVE]
Review the 'Compute Brain' of Google Cloud and its deployment options.

[CONCEPT EXPLANATION]
Choosing between Cloud Run and GKE is the most common architectural decision in modern GCP engineering. 

Key Service Matchings:
- App Engine: Standard for cost/zero-scaling, Flexible for custom binaries.
- Cloud Run: Best serverless container option. Portable and scales to zero.
- GKE: Pro choice for microservices. Use Autopilot for efficiency and Workload Identity for security.
- CI/CD: Artifact Registry (Storage) + Cloud Build (Automation).

[COMMANDS]
* `kubectl get deployments` # Final check of running workloads

[REAL-WORLD USE CASE]
Finalizing a migration from legacy VMs to a modern mixture of Cloud Run for APIs and GKE for stateful background processing.

[COMMON MISTAKES]
Thinking there is only one 'right' service. Most production environments use a combination of these services based on specific task needs.

[BEST PRACTICE]
Prioritize serverless (Cloud Run/Functions) for agility and shift to GKE only when orchestration complexity requires it.

[SUMMARY]
- App Engine for rapid web apps.
- Cloud Run for serverless containers.
- GKE for advanced orchestration.
- Artifact Registry and Cloud Build for CI/CD.
insight: Choosing between Cloud Run and GKE is the most common architectural decision in modern GCP engineering.
